theme: Who gets asked, who decides & tail latency

questions.concept: Collaborative shopping lists for multi-member households
questions.question: A quick-commerce app in India finds that in joint-family homes, three or four people message one 'buyer' on WhatsApp with items to order, and the buyer often forgets things. What is the best first product bet?
options: A shared household list that anyone can add to, which the buyer checks out in one tap
Let each family member place a separate order so nobody has to coordinate
Send the buyer daily push reminders listing the items they usually reorder
Add a WhatsApp chatbot that the buyer forwards family messages to for parsing
questions.explanation: The pain is coordination: requests scattered across chats get lost before reaching one payer. A shared list keeps the buyer as the decision-maker and payer, but lets everyone add items where the order actually happens. It keeps the existing social roles and removes the copying step.
rationales: Correct: it fixes the lost-request problem while keeping one buyer who pays and checks out.
Wrong: separate orders mean multiple delivery fees and break the family's norm of one person managing spending.
Wrong: reminders about past orders don't capture new requests from other family members, which is the actual gap.
Wrong: forwarding still relies on the buyer copying each message; it automates the symptom, not the coordination.
questions.interview_tip: In product-sense rounds, name the real job (coordinating many requesters and one payer) before solutioning. Strong answers keep existing social roles instead of fighting them.

questions.concept: Not relying on colour alone to convey status
questions.question: A B2B dashboard shows healthy, warning and failing services as green, amber and red dots only. Several customers say they 'can't tell which service is down'. What is the most direct fix?
options: Make the dots larger and use brighter shades of the same three colours
Add a text label or distinct icon shape to each status alongside its colour
Move failing services to a separate page so the main list shows only healthy ones
Add a legend at the top of the page explaining what each colour means
questions.explanation: About 1 in 12 men have some colour vision deficiency, and red/green are the hardest to tell apart. Status should be conveyed by at least two cues, such as colour plus a label or icon shape. This is a basic accessibility rule (WCAG 'use of colour') that also helps everyone scan faster.
rationales: Wrong: brighter red and green are still hard to tell apart for users with red-green colour deficiency.
Correct: a second cue like a label or shape works regardless of how users perceive colour.
Wrong: hiding failures on another page makes the most important status harder to find.
Wrong: a legend explains the colours but doesn't help users who can't distinguish them.
questions.interview_tip: Accessibility often appears as a follow-up in design questions. Mentioning 'never encode meaning in colour alone' shows you design for all users by default.

questions.concept: Closing the loop for job applicants on status
questions.question: You're the PM for a jobs marketplace. Research shows candidates' top complaint is 'ghosting': they never hear back after applying. Recruiters say they're too busy to reply to hundreds of applicants. What's the strongest solution?
options: Cap applications per job at 50 so recruiters have time to answer everyone personally
Show candidates a 'response rate' badge on each recruiter so they avoid unresponsive ones
Let recruiters close a job in one action that sends every unreviewed applicant a status update
Send candidates a weekly email suggesting new jobs so they feel engaged while waiting
questions.explanation: The constraint is recruiter effort, so the solution must make closing the loop nearly free for them. Tying a bulk status update to an action recruiters already take (closing or filling a role) gives candidates closure without new work. Badges and caps push the problem onto one side instead of removing the effort.
rationales: Wrong: a hard cap hurts both sides: recruiters lose good candidates and applicants lose access to jobs.
Wrong: badges may shift behaviour slowly but leave most candidates still unanswered and can punish busy recruiters.
Correct: it attaches closure to a step recruiters already do, so the loop closes at almost no cost to them.
Wrong: more job suggestions don't tell candidates what happened to their application, which is the actual pain.
questions.interview_tip: Marketplace design questions test whether you respect both sides' constraints. Strong answers find a change that costs the busy side almost nothing while solving the other side's pain.

questions.concept: Timing in-app review prompts after a success moment
questions.question: A ride-hailing app asks for an app-store review on app launch, and its store rating sits at 3.6 even though in-app ride ratings average 4.7. Where should the review prompt appear?
options: On every fifth app launch so more users see it and the sample gets larger
Right after a completed ride the user rated four or five stars
Inside the help section, so only engaged users who look for it will leave reviews
Immediately after a cancelled ride, to collect feedback while the experience is fresh
questions.explanation: Asking at launch catches users mid-task and annoyed, which biases ratings down. Prompting right after a successful, positively rated ride reaches users at a moment of delivered value. Platforms also limit how often the prompt can show, so it should be spent on the best moment.
rationales: Wrong: more launch prompts still interrupt users mid-task and keep the same negative bias.
Correct: it asks right after value is delivered, when the user just told you they were satisfied.
Wrong: almost nobody visits help to leave a review, and those who do are often having problems.
Wrong: a cancellation is a failure moment; prompting there would push the store rating even lower.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers like 'moment' questions because they test empathy for user context. Tie the timing to a success moment and mention rate limits on the prompt.

questions.concept: Choosing an inactivity threshold to define churn without subscriptions
questions.question: A free food-delivery app wants to report 'churned users', but users never cancel anything. How should the team define churn?
options: Any user who didn't order in the last 7 days, since weekly is a common reporting cadence
Any user who uninstalled the app, since that's the only explicit signal of leaving
Users past an inactivity window chosen where very few of them ever return to order again
Any user whose order count this month fell below their own average order count
questions.explanation: Without a cancel event, churn has to be inferred from inactivity. The right window comes from data: plot the chance of returning by days inactive, and pick the point where return rates flatten near zero. Too short a window labels normal gaps as churn; too long hides it.
rationales: Wrong: many healthy users order every 2-3 weeks, so a 7-day window would count them as churned.
Wrong: many inactive users never uninstall, so uninstalls badly undercount churn and are hard to track.
Correct: a data-driven window separates natural gaps from users who have really left.
Wrong: that measures declining engagement, not leaving; a user ordering less is still active.
questions.interview_tip: Defining metrics for non-subscription products is a common follow-up. Saying you'd pick the window from return-probability curves shows rigour, not guesswork.

questions.concept: Sampling change in who is asked behind a rating drop
questions.question: A food-delivery app's average order rating fell from 4.6 to 4.3 the week after it started asking every customer to rate, instead of only those who opened the 'rate order' screen. Complaints and refunds are flat. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Food quality dropped across restaurants that week, and the new prompt simply caught it
The new prompt has a UI bug that is recording ratings one star lower than tapped
Customers are annoyed by the new prompt and are punishing the app with low ratings
Who is rating changed: the old ratings came mostly from happy volunteers, the new ones from everyone
questions.explanation: When you change who is asked, you change the sample. Before, mainly delighted users chose to rate; now lukewarm users rate too, so the average falls even if experience is unchanged. Flat complaints and refunds support this. Compare like with like, such as ratings from users who would have opted in before.
rationales: Wrong: a real quality drop would usually show up in complaints and refunds too, which are flat.
Wrong: possible to check, but a uniform bug is less likely than the obvious sample change made the same week.
Wrong: annoyance can play a part, but the main effect is mathematical: a broader sample includes less-satisfied raters.
Correct: the change in who is asked explains the drop while other quality signals stay flat.
questions.interview_tip: Root-cause questions reward checking 'did the measurement change?' before 'did the product change?'. Naming selection effects and a like-for-like comparison is a strong signal.

questions.concept: Appeal overturn rate as a moderation precision signal
questions.question: A marketplace uses an automated system to remove listings that break its rules. Which metric best tells you whether it is removing too many legitimate listings?
options: Total number of listings removed per day by the system
Share of appealed removals that human reviewers overturn
Average time between a listing going live and being removed
Number of user reports filed against listings each day
questions.explanation: Overturned appeals are cases where the system removed something it should not have, so the overturn rate approximates false positives. Track it alongside how many sellers appeal, since many wrongly removed sellers never bother. Raw removal counts can't tell good removals from bad.
rationales: Wrong: removals could rise because of more violations or more mistakes; the count can't separate the two.
Correct: overturned appeals directly measure removals that were wrong, a precision signal.
Wrong: speed matters for harm reduction but says nothing about whether removals were correct.
Wrong: reports measure how much bad content users see, closer to recall, not wrongful removals.
questions.interview_tip: Trust and safety metric questions test precision vs recall thinking. Pairing a 'missed harm' metric with a 'wrongful action' metric like overturn rate is what interviewers look for.

questions.concept: Simple LTV formula from margin and churn
questions.question: A SaaS tool earns $20 per customer per month at a 75% gross margin, and loses 5% of customers each month. Using the simple formula, what is the gross-margin lifetime value per customer?
questions.explanation: Simple LTV = monthly ARPU × gross margin ÷ monthly churn. That is $20 × 0.75 = $15 of margin per month, and 1 ÷ 0.05 = 20 months average lifetime. $15 × 20 = $300.
rationales: Wrong: $400 is revenue lifetime value; it ignores the 75% gross margin.
Wrong: $225 applies the margin twice ($300 × 0.75).
Wrong: $15 is just one month of gross margin, not the lifetime value.
questions.interview_tip: Unit-economics questions often start with LTV. Using gross margin, not revenue, and stating the formula out loud shows financial fluency.

questions.concept: Probability to beat control in Bayesian A/B readouts
questions.question: Your experimentation tool reports a Bayesian result: 'Variant B has a 93% probability of beating control, expected lift +1.2%'. What is the correct interpretation?
options: Given the data and the prior, there is a 93% chance B's true effect is above zero
If we ran this test 100 times, B would win in exactly 93 of them
There is a 7% chance the result is a false positive, like a p-value of 0.07
B is guaranteed to lift the metric by at least 1.2% after launch
questions.explanation: A Bayesian posterior gives a direct probability statement about the true effect, given the data and prior assumptions. 93% to beat control still leaves a 7% chance B is worse, and the size of that possible loss matters. Teams often pair it with 'expected loss' to decide whether to ship.
rationales: Correct: that is exactly what a posterior probability of beating control means.
Wrong: that describes repeated-sampling frequencies, not what a posterior probability states.
Wrong: a p-value is a different quantity; 1 minus the posterior probability is not a p-value.
Wrong: +1.2% is an expected value with uncertainty around it, not a guaranteed minimum.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers check whether you can explain results to stakeholders without overclaiming. Contrast it with a p-value and mention expected loss for extra credit.

questions.concept: Page-level randomization for SEO experiments
questions.question: A travel site wants to test new title tags on its 40,000 city pages to see if they bring more Google search traffic. Why can't it run a normal user-level A/B test?
options: Search engines block sites from running any A/B tests on pages they index
User-level tests need logged-in users, and most search visitors are logged out
Title tags change too rarely for the test to reach significance in a few weeks
The 'user' here is the search engine's single crawler, so you split pages into groups instead
questions.explanation: Search ranking is decided by one crawler seeing one version of each page, so you can't show different users different versions and measure organic traffic. Instead, split similar pages into control and test groups, change only the test group, and compare traffic trends, often against a forecast from pre-period data.
rationales: Wrong: search engines allow testing; they discourage cloaking, which is showing crawlers different content from users.
Wrong: user-level tests can use cookies for logged-out users; login isn't the problem.
Wrong: test length is a planning issue; the core problem is the randomization unit.
Correct: the outcome depends on what the crawler sees, so pages, not users, must be the unit.
questions.interview_tip: Choosing the randomization unit is a favourite experimentation question. Recognising that the 'treated' party is the crawler, not the user, shows deep understanding.

questions.concept: Annual AC servicing visits in Delhi
questions.question: Roughly how many air-conditioner servicing visits happen in Delhi each year?
options: About 45 thousand
About 4.5 lakh
About 45 lakh
About 4.5 crore
questions.explanation: Delhi has about 2.2 crore people, roughly 50 lakh households at ~4.4 per home. Assume about 40% own ACs, so ~20 lakh homes, with ~1.5 ACs each, giving ~30 lakh ACs. At about 1.5 services per AC per year (pre-summer plus repairs), that's ~45 lakh visits. Offices and shops would add more.
rationales: Wrong: 45 thousand would mean only a tiny share of ACs ever get serviced.
Wrong: 4.5 lakh implies one service per AC every six or seven years, far below normal practice.
Correct: households × AC ownership × ACs per home × services per year ≈ 45 lakh.
Wrong: 4.5 crore would need about 15 services per AC per year.
questions.interview_tip: For guesstimates, state the structure first (households, ownership, units, frequency), then sanity-check. Mentioning segments you excluded, like offices, shows awareness of scope.

questions.concept: Time-saved estimate for an AI meeting notetaker
questions.question: A 10,000-person company is considering an AI meeting notetaker. About 60% of staff attend meetings regularly, and the tool saves each of them roughly 15 minutes a day on notes and follow-ups. About how many hours does it save company-wide per week?
options: About 750 hours
About 7,500 hours
About 60,000 hours
About 75,000 hours
questions.explanation: 6,000 users × 15 minutes × 5 days = 450,000 minutes, or 7,500 hours per week. That is about 190 full-time weeks of work. The key is applying the saving only to meeting attendees and only to note-taking time, not to the whole meeting.
rationales: Wrong: 750 hours is ten times too low, probably from dropping a factor like the five working days.
Correct: 6,000 × 0.25 hours × 5 days = 7,500 hours.
Wrong: about 60,000 hours assumes the tool saves all meeting time, not just note-taking.
Wrong: 75,000 hours is ten times too high, probably applying 15 minutes per meeting rather than per day.
questions.interview_tip: Value-based estimates often back an AI business case. Interviewers look for whether you count only the time the tool actually replaces, not the whole activity.

questions.concept: Buyer power from a few large retail customers
questions.question: A packaged-snacks brand sells 70% of its volume through three large retail chains. In Porter's Five Forces, what does this mainly indicate?
options: High buyer power, since a few big buyers can push down prices and demand better terms
High supplier power, since the brand depends on retailers to supply shelf space
High threat of new entrants, since retail chains can easily stock rival snacks
Low competitive rivalry, since three chains limit how many brands reach consumers
questions.explanation: Buyer power is high when a few buyers account for a large share of sales. Losing one chain would hit the brand hard, so the chains can demand lower prices, promotions and listing fees. Brands reduce this by building direct channels or strong consumer pull.
rationales: Correct: concentrated customers have strong bargaining power over the seller.
Wrong: the retailers are the brand's customers (buyers), not its suppliers.
Wrong: entrant threat is about new competitors entering the market, not where sales are concentrated.
Wrong: rivalry between snack brands for limited shelf space is, if anything, intensified.
questions.interview_tip: Five Forces questions test whether you can map a real situation to the right force. Following with a mitigation, like direct channels, shows you think strategically, not just academically.

questions.concept: Scaling a negative-unit-economics business amplifies losses
questions.question: A startup loses ₹40 on every delivery after delivery costs, and its plan is to 'grow fast and get profitable at scale'. What should a PM check first?
options: Whether the marketing budget can double so the company grows fast
Whether competitors are also losing money, so the market stays healthy
Whether app ratings are high enough to support a higher price later
Which specific costs fall with scale, and whether that closes the ₹40 gap
questions.explanation: If each order loses money, more orders just mean bigger losses unless scale changes the per-order economics. You need a concrete path: denser routes, larger basket sizes, cheaper buying, or fees. If no cost actually falls with volume, growth makes things worse.
rationales: Wrong: spending more to grow faster increases losses if each order is still negative.
Wrong: competitors' losses don't fix your unit economics and can mean a price war.
Wrong: ratings matter, but the first question is whether any lever makes each order profitable.
Correct: profitability at scale requires specific per-order costs that actually fall with volume.
questions.interview_tip: Business questions often hide a unit-economics trap. Asking 'what changes per order at scale?' shows you won't confuse growth with health.

questions.concept: Prioritising markets by attractiveness and ability to win
questions.question: An Indian payments startup must pick its first international market. Indonesia is the largest market; the UAE is smaller but has a large Indian diaspora already using the product for remittances, and partner banks there have reached out. Which reasoning is strongest?
options: Pick Indonesia, since the biggest addressable market always offers the most upside
Pick whichever market has the fewest competitors, since less competition means faster growth
Weigh market size against ability to win; the UAE's existing users and partners may beat a larger, harder market
Enter both at once so the company doesn't miss either window
questions.explanation: Market choice should weigh how attractive a market is (size, growth, margins) against your ability to win there (existing users, distribution, partners, regulation). A smaller market where you start with demand and partners can be a better first step than a huge market where you start from zero. Early wins also fund later expansion.
rationales: Wrong: size matters, but a large market you can't win is worth less than a smaller one you can.
Wrong: few competitors can also mean little demand or high barriers; it's one factor, not the decision.
Correct: it balances attractiveness with concrete advantages that raise the odds of winning.
Wrong: splitting a startup's limited team across two launches usually weakens both.
questions.interview_tip: Market-entry questions reward a two-axis framework (attractiveness × ability to win). Using evidence from the prompt, like existing users and inbound partners, makes the answer concrete.

questions.concept: Single-threaded owner for a critical initiative
questions.question: A checkout redesign has stalled for two quarters because four teams each own a piece and nobody owns the whole result. What is Amazon's 'single-threaded leader' fix?
options: Add a weekly sync where all four team leads share status updates
Have the VP review progress personally every week
Give one leader full-time ownership of the result, with the authority and team to deliver it
Split the project into four separate launches so each team ships independently
questions.explanation: A single-threaded leader works only on one initiative and is accountable for its outcome, usually with a dedicated team. When ownership is split, everyone optimises their part and the whole drifts. Status meetings and exec reviews add visibility but not ownership.
rationales: Wrong: more syncs share status but still leave no one accountable for the overall result.
Wrong: exec attention helps briefly but a VP can't own day-to-day trade-offs across teams.
Correct: one dedicated owner with authority removes the gap where no one owns the whole.
Wrong: separate launches may produce a fragmented checkout that no one is responsible for end to end.
questions.interview_tip: Amazon interviews often probe ownership structures. Explaining why split ownership stalls work, and how you'd fix it, shows organisational maturity.

questions.concept: Reference-class forecasting to counter the planning fallacy
questions.question: Your team estimates a data migration at 6 weeks. The last four similar migrations in the company took 10, 12, 9 and 14 weeks, each estimated at about 6. What's the best way to set the plan?
options: Keep 6 weeks, since this team is more experienced than the previous ones
Use 6 weeks but add a 10% buffer for unexpected issues
Ask the team to re-estimate in more detail until everyone agrees on a number
Anchor on past similar migrations (about 9-14 weeks) and adjust for real differences
questions.explanation: The planning fallacy is our tendency to underestimate our own tasks. Reference-class forecasting fixes it by starting from how long similar projects actually took, then adjusting for specific differences. Bottom-up detail tends to miss the same unknowns again.
rationales: Wrong: every team believes it is the exception; that belief is the planning fallacy itself.
Wrong: a 10% buffer is tiny compared with the 50-130% overruns seen on past migrations.
Wrong: more detailed bottom-up estimates usually miss the same unknown problems as before.
Correct: base rates from similar projects are the best starting point, then you adjust.
questions.interview_tip: When asked how you handle estimates, citing base rates from similar past work shows you plan with evidence, not optimism.

questions.concept: Combining top-down goals with bottom-up plans in planning
questions.question: Leadership sets a goal to grow paid conversions 20% next year. Your team's bottom-up plan of known projects adds up to about 8%. What is the best next step?
options: Commit to 20% anyway and figure out how during the year
Show the 12-point gap and propose options: extra bets, more resources, or a revised target
Submit the 8% plan quietly and let leadership notice the difference
Pad each project's impact estimate until the total reaches 20%
questions.explanation: Good planning reconciles top-down ambition with bottom-up reality. Making the gap visible lets leadership decide: fund new bets, add people, accept risk, or change the goal. Hiding or papering over the gap guarantees a surprise later.
rationales: Wrong: committing without a plan sets up a predictable miss and erodes trust.
Correct: it surfaces the gap early with concrete choices so leaders can make a real trade-off.
Wrong: staying silent avoids the hard conversation now and creates a worse one later.
Wrong: inflating estimates hides the gap and damages your credibility when results arrive.
questions.interview_tip: Planning questions test candour with leadership. Strong answers quantify the gap and bring options, not just a problem.

questions.concept: Addressing a high performer's disrespectful behaviour
questions.question: Your strongest engineer ships the most code, but often dismisses junior teammates' ideas harshly in design reviews. Two juniors have stopped speaking up. As the PM partnering with the eng manager, what's the best approach?
options: Leave it alone, since output matters most and the engineer's results speak for themselves
Raise it publicly in the next review so the whole team sees the standard
Ask the juniors to toughen up and defend their ideas more firmly
Work with the eng manager so specific examples and their impact are raised with the engineer privately
questions.explanation: Behaviour that silences others has a hidden cost: lost ideas and a team that stops contributing. The eng manager owns performance feedback, so the PM should bring specific examples and impact to them and support a private conversation. Strong cultures hold high performers to the same behaviour bar.
rationales: Wrong: the team's lost contributions are a real cost that the engineer's output doesn't offset.
Wrong: public correction humiliates and usually makes people defensive rather than changing behaviour.
Wrong: it puts the burden on the people being harmed instead of addressing the cause.
Correct: it respects who owns feedback and gives the engineer concrete, private, actionable input.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers want to see you won't trade team health for one person's output. Naming who owns the feedback, and giving specifics, shows judgement.

questions.concept: Re-motivating a team after a failed launch
questions.question: A feature your team spent five months on launched and missed every target; leadership is pausing it. Morale is low and people are asking if their work mattered. What's the best way to lead the team forward?
options: Hold an honest review of what you learned, credit good work, and connect the lessons to the next bet
Move straight to the next project so the team stops dwelling on the failure
Explain that leadership's decision was premature and the feature would have worked with more time
Tell the team the targets were unrealistic, so the miss wasn't really their fault
questions.explanation: After a failure, teams need to hear the truth, see what was learned, and know their effort was valued. A blameless review turns the work into insight, and tying it to the next decision shows it mattered. Skipping or deflecting leaves cynicism behind.
rationales: Correct: honesty, recognition and a link to what's next rebuild motivation on solid ground.
Wrong: skipping reflection wastes the lessons and leaves people feeling their work was discarded.
Wrong: undermining leadership may feel supportive but breeds cynicism and doesn't move the team forward.
Wrong: blaming the targets avoids ownership and teaches nothing about what to do differently.
questions.interview_tip: Failure stories are common in behavioural rounds. Strong answers show ownership, specific learnings, and how you turned them into the next result.

questions.concept: Removing yourself as a decision bottleneck through delegation
questions.question: Your team of eight waits on you to approve every copy change, design tweak and minor scope call. Velocity has dropped and you're working weekends. What's the best fix?
options: Work longer hours for a few weeks to clear the approval backlog
Hire another PM so approvals are split across two people
Define which decisions the team owns, share the principles you use, and review outcomes instead of approving each call
Stop reviewing small decisions entirely and let the team ship whatever they choose
questions.explanation: A PM who approves everything becomes the slowest part of the system. Clear decision rights plus shared principles (who the user is, the quality bar, what matters most) let the team decide well on their own. You then check outcomes and coach, which scales far better than gatekeeping.
rationales: Wrong: extra hours treat the symptom and won't last; the bottleneck returns.
Wrong: a second approver halves the queue but keeps the same broken structure.
Correct: it pushes decisions to the team with guardrails, removing the bottleneck sustainably.
Wrong: removing all guidance risks inconsistent quality; delegation needs clear principles, not absence.
questions.interview_tip: Scaling yourself is a key senior-PM signal. Describing decision rights and principles, not just 'trusting the team', shows a repeatable mechanism.

questions.concept: Long-context stuffing vs RAG for large document sets
questions.question: A legal-tech startup lets lawyers ask questions across a firm's 50,000 contracts. An engineer suggests skipping retrieval and putting everything into a model with a 1M-token context window. What's the main problem?
options: Long-context models can't read legal language as accurately as short-context models
Context windows can't hold scanned PDFs, only plain text
Retrieval is always more accurate than long context, regardless of corpus size
50,000 contracts far exceed 1M tokens, and sending huge contexts on every question is slow and costly
questions.explanation: Even large windows hold a few thousand pages at most, while 50,000 contracts are hundreds of millions of tokens. Sending massive contexts on each query also drives up cost and latency. Retrieval narrows the input to relevant passages; long context works well once you've retrieved a manageable set.
rationales: Wrong: there's no evidence that long-context models handle legal text worse in general.
Wrong: PDFs are converted to text or images first; format isn't the core limit.
Wrong: long context can beat retrieval for small corpora; the issue here is scale and cost.
Correct: the corpus is far too large, and per-query cost and latency would be very high.
questions.interview_tip: AI PM interviews often ask RAG vs long-context. A strong answer does quick token math and treats them as complementary rather than rivals.

questions.concept: Jailbreaks vs prompt injection
questions.question: What's the key difference between a jailbreak and a prompt injection attack on an AI assistant?
options: Jailbreaks target image models, while prompt injections target text models
A jailbreak is when the user tries to bypass safety rules; an injection hides instructions in content the model reads
Prompt injection only works on open-weights models, while jailbreaks work on any model
Jailbreaks require access to the system prompt, while injections don't
questions.explanation: In a jailbreak, the user directly tries to get the model to break its rules. In prompt injection, attacker instructions are hidden in third-party content (a web page, email, document) that the model processes on the user's behalf. Injection is the bigger risk for agents, because the user may be the victim, not the attacker.
rationales: Wrong: both attacks apply to text and multimodal models.
Correct: the difference is who supplies the malicious instruction and through which channel.
Wrong: both attacks affect closed and open models alike.
Wrong: neither attack requires seeing the system prompt.
questions.interview_tip: Knowing who the attacker is in each case shows security fluency. Link injection risk to agents with tools for a strong answer.

questions.concept: Decomposing a task into a prompt chain
questions.question: A single long prompt that reads a support ticket, classifies it, looks up policy and drafts a reply is unreliable, and it's hard to tell which part fails. What's the best change?
options: Split it into a chain of smaller steps, each with its own output you can check and evaluate
Add more examples to the single prompt until the failures stop
Raise the temperature so the model explores more ways to solve the task
Switch to the largest available model and keep the single prompt as is
questions.explanation: Breaking a complex task into steps (classify, retrieve policy, draft) makes each step simpler and gives you checkpoints. You can evaluate and fix each step separately and use cheaper models where possible. The trade-off is more calls and a bit more latency.
rationales: Correct: smaller steps are easier to get right, test and debug individually.
Wrong: more examples may help a bit but still leave one opaque prompt that's hard to debug.
Wrong: higher temperature adds randomness, which usually makes reliability worse.
Wrong: a bigger model may help but costs more and still hides which step is failing.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers like seeing debuggability as a design goal. Mention per-step evals and the latency trade-off for a complete answer.

questions.concept: Freezing the judge model version for comparable eval scores
questions.question: Your team scores a writing assistant weekly using an LLM judge. This week every variant's score jumped 6 points, including the unchanged baseline. The judge points to the provider's 'latest' model alias. What most likely happened, and what's the fix?
options: Users are writing better prompts, so pin the evaluation set to older prompts
The baseline quietly improved, so update the baseline and keep comparing
The judge model was updated behind the alias; pin a fixed judge version and re-score the baseline
LLM judges are random, so average scores over more weeks before acting
questions.explanation: If an unchanged baseline moves, the measuring tool changed. A 'latest' alias can silently switch to a new model that grades differently. Pin the judge to a specific version, re-run the baseline on it, and treat any judge upgrade as a deliberate, recalibrated change.
rationales: Wrong: weekly evals use a fixed set; user prompts in production don't change eval inputs.
Wrong: the baseline didn't change, so its score shouldn't have; the grader is the variable.
Correct: an unpinned judge is the classic cause of a uniform shift across all variants.
Wrong: some noise exists, but a uniform 6-point jump for all variants points to a systematic change.
questions.interview_tip: Eval reliability questions test whether you treat the grader as part of the system. Saying 'an unchanged baseline moving means the ruler moved' is a crisp signal.

questions.concept: On-device vs cloud inference trade-off
questions.question: A keyboard app wants AI next-phrase suggestions as users type. Why might it run a small model on the phone rather than call a large cloud model?
options: On-device models are always more accurate than cloud models
Cloud models can't handle short text like keyboard input
On-device inference has no cost to the company and no battery impact for users
It gives instant suggestions offline and keeps typed text on the device, at some cost to quality
questions.explanation: Suggestions need to appear within milliseconds as users type, and a network round trip is too slow and fails offline. Keeping keystrokes on the phone is also a major privacy win. The trade-offs are smaller models with lower quality and some battery and storage use.
rationales: Wrong: small on-device models are usually less capable than large cloud models.
Wrong: cloud models handle short text fine; latency and privacy are the issues.
Wrong: on-device inference uses battery and storage, and building small models still costs money.
Correct: latency, offline use and privacy favour on-device, with a quality trade-off.
questions.interview_tip: AI architecture questions reward naming the constraints that drive the choice. Latency, privacy, offline use and cost are the four to cover.

questions.concept: Storing timestamps in UTC
questions.question: A booking app stores appointment times in each server's local time. After expanding from India to the UAE, customers see wrong times. What's the standard fix?
options: Store all times in UTC and convert to each user's time zone only when displaying
Store all times in India Standard Time, since that's where the company is based
Ask users to enter times in the server's time zone when booking
Run separate servers in each country so local time always matches users
questions.explanation: Storing time in one universal reference (UTC) avoids confusion across servers, regions and daylight-saving changes. The app converts to the user's or venue's time zone only for display. For future appointments, also store the intended local time zone so changes in rules don't shift them.
rationales: Correct: UTC storage plus conversion on display is the standard approach.
Wrong: a single local zone still breaks for users elsewhere and for zones with daylight saving.
Wrong: asking users to do conversion is error-prone and a poor experience.
Wrong: separate servers don't solve cross-border bookings and add a lot of complexity.
questions.interview_tip: Simple technical questions check you understand common data pitfalls. Mentioning storing the venue's time zone for future events shows extra depth.

questions.concept: Tail latency amplification in fan-out requests
questions.question: A home-feed request calls 50 backend services in parallel and waits for all of them. Each service is fast 99% of the time but slow 1% of the time. Roughly what share of feed loads will be slow?
options: About 1%, since each service is slow only 1% of the time
About 2%, since slow calls in parallel overlap
About 40%, since the chance at least one of 50 calls is slow is high
About 50%, since each of the 50 services adds 1%
questions.explanation: The chance that all 50 calls are fast is 0.99^50, about 0.61, so about 39% of requests hit at least one slow call. When you wait for the slowest of many calls, rare slowness becomes common. Fixes include timeouts with partial results, hedged requests, and fewer dependencies.
rationales: Wrong: that's true for one call, but waiting on 50 calls multiplies the exposure.
Wrong: parallel calls don't overlap away slowness; one slow call delays the whole request.
Correct: 1 − 0.99^50 ≈ 39%, so roughly 40% of feed loads are slow.
Wrong: probabilities don't add linearly; the correct figure is about 39%.
questions.interview_tip: This 'tail at scale' idea appears in system-design discussions. Doing the quick probability and proposing partial-result timeouts shows strong technical fluency.

questions.concept: Launching in an atomic network before expanding
questions.question: A new neighbourhood-services app (plumbers, tutors, cooks) has small amounts of supply and demand spread across all of Bengaluru, and few requests get matched. What's the best growth move?
options: Spend more on city-wide ads to increase total sign-ups on both sides
Add more service categories so every user finds something useful
Focus on a few neighbourhoods until supply and demand are dense enough for matches
Expand to Pune and Hyderabad to show investors the model scales
questions.explanation: Local marketplaces work only when there's enough density in each area for buyers to find sellers quickly. Concentrating on a small 'atomic network' (a few neighbourhoods) makes matches happen, which drives word of mouth. Then you expand area by area.
rationales: Wrong: city-wide spend spreads users thin again, so match rates stay low.
Wrong: more categories divide already thin supply further.
Correct: building density in a small area is what makes local network effects start working.
Wrong: new cities repeat the thin-density problem before it's solved in the first one.
questions.interview_tip: Marketplace growth questions often test density thinking. Naming the 'atomic network' and showing how you'd expand from it is a strong signal.

questions.concept: ChatGPT ads kept separate from answer generation (Oct 2026)
questions.question: In October 2026, OpenAI described how ChatGPT picks ads: the ad system runs on separate services, models and code from the system that writes answers, a model only nominates candidates, and an auction tool decides placement. Why design it this way?
options: Regulators require AI companies to run advertising on physically separate data centres
Separate systems let OpenAI charge advertisers more by running two auctions per query
A single combined model would be too large to serve, so the split is purely about compute
It protects trust that ads don't shape answers, and an ad outage or delay doesn't slow replies
questions.explanation: Reports on OpenAI's post say ad services, models and code are separate from answer generation, so a slow or failing ad system doesn't delay responses, and ads appear below replies. OpenAI says ads do not shape ChatGPT's answers, and the auction, not the language model, decides placement and price. The PM lesson: when monetisation could threaten the core product's trust, separate them architecturally.
rationales: Wrong: the reports cite no such regulation; the separation is OpenAI's own design choice.
Wrong: nothing reported suggests double auctions; the auction tool makes one placement and pricing decision.
Wrong: compute isn't the stated reason; independence of answers and reliability are.
Correct: separation protects answer integrity and keeps ad problems from delaying responses.
questions.interview_tip: Monetisation questions for AI assistants often ask how to add ads without losing trust. Citing architectural separation and keeping the core experience independent is a strong, current answer.
